Lesson Overview: Putting It All Together—Unit 6 Synthesis

Lesson Focus

Lesson 8: Putting It All Together—Unit 6 Synthesis

This lesson integrates previously taught standards in portfolio selection and reflection, revision from feedback, format-specific publication, online publication, author presentation, and craft reasoning. No new primary standard is introduced.

What You Will Learn

  • Synthesize the full author-portfolio process under unfamiliar constraints.
  • Choose among competing editorial, ethical, design, and presentation priorities.
  • Trace every major claim to verifiable portfolio evidence.
  • Prepare for the Unit 6 Final Assessment and final course-quality review.

Why This Matters

Creative writing helps you communicate ideas, experiences, and perspectives with purpose. Each lesson strengthens your ability to read like a writer, make deliberate craft choices, revise thoughtfully, and explain how those choices affect a reader. These skills build creative confidence, clear communication, and responsible participation in a writing community.

What You Will Do

  • Learn and apply the lesson vocabulary.
  • Follow step-by-step instruction and study worked examples.
  • Practice through interactive checks and guided application.
  • Complete Independent Work to apply the lesson skills.
  • Complete a separate Checkpoint to demonstrate your understanding.

Lesson Workflow

  1. Complete Pages 1–4 in order.
  2. Complete Page 5 and submit it with your Page 2 vocabulary in Notebook Evidence Submission.
  3. Complete Page 6 and submit it separately in Checkpoint Submission.
  4. Review TOR feedback, correct errors, and resubmit any work scoring below 80%.
  5. Complete the assessment listed after the lesson. A score of at least 80% is required.

page.title: Vocabulary and Definitions
page.contents:
Creative Writing | Unit 6 | Lesson 8 | Page 2 of 6

Vocabulary and Definitions

Notebook Task: Record every core term and its complete meaning in your notebook. Submit these vocabulary notes with your Independent Work as Notebook Evidence. Use the examples to see how each term works in context. Reference glossary terms do not need to be copied.
TermMeaningExample
synthesisThe integration of multiple skills or ideas into a coherent new judgment or product.The final defense combines craft analysis, evidence, and reflection.
constraint hierarchyA ranking of requirements according to importance, risk, and dependency.Permission and accessibility come before decorative design choices.
evidence chainA connected sequence from claim to artifact, exact evidence, reasoning, and verification.The defense links a growth claim to paired drafts and explains the change.
authenticityThe credible alignment of a writer’s voice, choices, values, and evidence.The statement honestly explains both success and unresolved risk.
editorial independenceThe ability to evaluate feedback and make reasoned decisions rather than obeying every suggestion.The writer rejects advice that would erase the intended ambiguity.
quality thresholdThe minimum defined level a product must meet before release.Every link must function and every source must have permission.
risk mitigationAn action that reduces the likelihood or impact of a known problem.Keeping a verified backup reduces the risk of losing the final files.
summative assessmentAn evaluation measuring integrated learning after instruction.The final portfolio defense is a summative assessment.
transfer taskA problem requiring learned skills to be applied in a new context.The writer applies revision criteria to an unfamiliar draft.

Vocabulary in Action

Match each clue to the precise term. Choose Check, study any mismatch, and retry. This practice is ungraded.

Make the Vocabulary Work

Which response builds a complete evidence chain?

A. “My portfolio shows growth because the final pieces are better.”

This gives a claim but no precise artifact, evidence, or reasoning.

B. “The first and final scene drafts show that I replaced summary with dialogue; the added conflict now makes the turning point earned.”

Correct. It identifies the artifacts, names the exact change, and explains how that evidence supports the claim.

page.title: Lesson
page.contents:
Creative Writing | Unit 6 | Lesson 8 | Page 3 of 6

Lesson: Make Defensible Decisions Across the Whole Portfolio

1. Establish the Nonnegotiables

Separate requirements (standards, rights, privacy, accessibility, file function) from preferences (color, ordering options, decorative style). Requirements set the quality threshold.

2. Rank Constraints and Dependencies

PriorityExamplesReason
1 Safety/ethicsConsent, privacy, rightsMay block publication entirely
2 Meaning/alignmentCorrect versions and evidenceDetermines validity
3 Access/functionContrast, transcripts, linksDetermines usability
4 PolishConsistency and surface errorsRefines an already valid product

Evidence Chain

Claim: what the portfolio demonstrates.
Artifact: which work carries the claim.
Exact evidence: where the feature appears.
Reasoning: how the feature supports purpose or growth.
Verification: how you confirmed the final reader receives the correct version.

Pause and Choose: Rank the Highest-Level Problem

A portfolio has elegant formatting, but one published image lacks permission and identifies a private person. What should be addressed first?

A. Adjust font consistency before release because visual polish is most noticeable.
Weaker choice. Polish cannot make an ethically invalid release acceptable. The rights and privacy problem may block publication entirely.
B. Remove or replace the image until permission, privacy, and school requirements are satisfied; then complete lower-priority polish.
Stronger choice. This follows the dependency order: safety and ethics first, then validity, access, and polish.

Retry: If your first choice is weaker, close it and select the other choice before continuing. Compare both explanations so you can name why the stronger answer works.

4. Resolve Feedback Conflicts

  1. Name the shared reader observation beneath conflicting advice.
  2. Return to purpose, audience, and evidence.
  3. Generate at least two revision options.
  4. Test both against the intended effect.
  5. Choose, adapt, or reject feedback with a documented rationale.

5. Apply a Release Decision

Choose Ready, Ready after named corrections, or Not ready. Support the judgment with evidence from craft, revision, alignment, publication, accessibility, rights, and presentation.

Pause and Choose: Make the Release Decision

The portfolio’s craft and evidence pass, but the final PDF contains two broken links and a missing audio transcript. Which judgment is defensible?

A. “Ready after named corrections”: repair and retest the links, add the transcript, and verify the new export.
Stronger choice. The underlying work is valid, but the reader-facing release still fails access and function. The judgment names exact corrections and verification.
B. “Ready” because content quality matters and technical problems can be ignored.
Weaker choice. Publication readiness includes the actual reader experience. Broken navigation and missing access support contradict a full-ready judgment.

Retry: If your first choice is weaker, close it and select the other choice before continuing. Compare both explanations so you can name why the stronger answer works.

Assessment Strategy

On a new scenario, do not choose the most polished-sounding answer automatically. Identify the highest-level problem, eliminate choices that ignore evidence or ethics, then select the action with the strongest causal connection to improvement.

page.title: Worked Example
page.contents:
Creative Writing | Unit 6 | Lesson 8 | Page 4 of 6

Worked Example: Three Unit 6 Transfer Problems

Example 1 — Competing Priorities

Case: A polished portfolio contains an interview without consent and a poem with one typographical error.

  1. Rank risk: missing consent can block publication; the typo is lower risk.
  2. Pause publication of the interview.
  3. Request and document consent or remove the media.
  4. Correct the typo afterward.
  5. Judgment: not ready until the rights issue is resolved.

Pause and Choose: A or B

Which issue must be resolved before the portfolio is ready to publish?

A. Correct the poem’s typographical error first because visible mistakes always create the greatest risk.
Weaker response. The typo affects polish, but it does not outweigh a rights and consent problem that can block ethical publication.
B. Pause publication of the interview until consent is documented or the media is removed; correct the lower-risk typo afterward.
Stronger response. This response ranks risks, protects the interview subject, names two acceptable remedies, and sequences lower-risk polishing afterward.

Retry: Close your first choice and open the other. Compare both explanations before continuing.

Example 2 — Feedback Conflict

Case: One reader wants an essay’s ending explained; another values its ambiguity.

  1. Shared observation: the ending requires interpretation.
  2. Purpose: invite uncertainty while preserving emotional clarity.
  3. Option A adds explanation; Option B strengthens an earlier recurring object.
  4. Test whether B gives readers a stable emotional relationship without one fixed meaning.
  5. Choose B if the evidence supports purposeful ambiguity.

Example 3 — Weak Evidence Chain

Claim: “I grew in characterization.” Evidence: a final excerpt only.

  1. Identify the missing links: no earlier version, diagnosis, or revision cause.
  2. Add a before passage where motive is stated abstractly.
  3. Add the after passage where choice and consequence reveal motive.
  4. Explain how feedback exposed the problem.
  5. Verify that the after passage appears in the released artifact.

Transfer Frame

Requirement → risk → evidence → options → test → decision → verification.

Your Turn Before Independent Work

Pause and try: A portfolio has perfect formatting but one image lacks permission. Decide readiness and state the next action.

Check your thinking — open after you try
Teacher model: The portfolio is not ready. Remove the image temporarily or obtain and record permission before publication; formatting quality cannot substitute for publication rights.

page.title: Independent Work
page.contents:
Creative Writing | Unit 6 | Lesson 8 | Page 5 of 6

Independent Work: Putting It All Together: Unit 6 Synthesis

Purpose

Synthesize the entire course into a polished, defensible author portfolio and presentation package.

Complete each numbered part in your notebook. Support decisions with precise evidence from your portfolio work.

Source for Your Work

Final synthesis role: You are curating a public-facing record of your development as an author. The finished portfolio must demonstrate achievement, growth, intentional craft, ethical publication, and readiness to communicate with an audience.

1. Plan Before You Work

Portfolio DecisionEvidence and Plan
Purpose and intended audienceState each precisely.
Strongest current evidenceName the piece, passage, or feature.
Most important improvementDescribe the needed change and intended effect.

2. Choose and Explain

Which approach demonstrates stronger author decision-making? Record A or B, then explain your choice in 2–3 sentences using a lesson concept.

A. Treat the portfolio as a storage folder that proves all required work was completed.
B. Treat the portfolio as an authored experience in which selection, revision, reflection, design, and presentation make a coherent argument about growth.

3. Apply the Lesson

Complete the final author portfolio: three or more polished creative works representing range, a 400–500 word author statement, craft rationales, documented revision evidence, coherent and accessible publication design, and a rehearsed five-minute presentation. Every claim must connect to specific portfolio evidence.

4. Revise with Purpose

Conduct a final four-pass audit for content, coherence, craft, and publication readiness. Document one consequential improvement from each pass and write a 200–250 word defense of why the portfolio is ready for an authentic audience.

Before You Submit

  • All four numbered parts are complete.
  • Your work applies the lesson skill to specific portfolio evidence.
  • Your explanation identifies a decision and its effect on the audience.
  • Your revision meaningfully improves quality, coherence, or readiness.

page.title: Checkpoint
page.contents:
Checkpoint: Putting It All Together: Unit 6 Synthesis

Put the lesson together through analysis, decision-making, writing, and purposeful revision.

Purpose

Show that you can understand the lesson concept, apply it in original work, and explain your decisions. Complete every numbered item and submit your responses with your Checkpoint work.

New Source: Final Editorial Review

Hours before a public portfolio showcase, an author discovers that one selected piece no longer represents the collection’s strongest work, the author statement describes an earlier sequence, a credited image is missing permission documentation, and the presentation link opens an outdated file.

A capstone synthesis demonstrates independent control by coordinating selection, revision, reflection, publication, ethics, accessibility, and presentation into a finished body of work.

Part 1: Analyze the Source

  1. Prioritize the four problems and justify the order using ethics, audience access, coherence, and quality.
  2. Explain what evidence would prove that the final portfolio represents both polished achievement and genuine growth.

Use this response pattern: Make a precise claim, cite the relevant detail, and explain how the detail proves the claim.

Part 2: Choose A or B

3. Which response demonstrates responsible capstone decision-making?

A. Keep the portfolio unchanged because last-minute consistency is more important than accuracy or ethics.
B. Resolve permission and file-authority risks, update the selection and framing together, then complete a documented final audience check.

Record A or B in your submission and explain your choice in 2–3 sentences. The answer is not revealed here because this item is part of your graded written work.

Part 3: Create and Apply

4. Submit a complete Creative Writing Capstone Portfolio and Presentation.

  1. Portfolio: Include at least five polished works in multiple forms, selected for quality, range, risk, and growth.
  2. Revision evidence: Provide a concise change record and before-and-after evidence for every work.
  3. Author statement: Write 500–700 words with a clear throughline, specific craft evidence, growth analysis, and next direction.
  4. Publication: Apply a professional, accessible design with verified navigation, attribution, permissions, and authoritative file versions.
  5. Presentation: Deliver or submit an 8–10 minute script with hook, throughline, selected excerpts, craft analysis, revision evidence, synthesis, and audience question.

Add a 300–400 word final reflection explaining how your strongest choices across the course work together and identifying one specific future goal.

Plan before drafting: Decide what the audience should understand, how each section will build that understanding, and which details will do the most work.

Part 4: Revise With Purpose

5. Conduct three final audits—content and coherence, ethics and accessibility, and technical delivery. Correct every issue found and document the three highest-impact changes.

Do more than correct spelling. Revise organization, meaning, evidence, or craft so the work becomes clearer and more effective.

Before You Submit

  • Every numbered item is complete.
  • Analysis includes specific evidence and reasoning.
  • The creative work follows the required organization and length.
  • The A/B response is recorded and explained.
  • The revision is visible and its purpose is clear.

Mastery Target

A score of 80% or higher demonstrates mastery. Depth, control, and application matter more than unnecessary length.

TOR Help

If you are unsure how to organize your response, choose evidence, or revise meaningfully, contact your Teacher of Record before submitting.
